sentences.text: The only known specimen of Dystrophaeus viaemalae is a single fragmentary holotype labeled USNM 2364.
Recent excavations uncovered additional parts of the specimen, including a phalanx, teeth, and vertebrae from the back and tail.
Dystrophaeus may have been approximately 13 meters long with a mass of roughly 7 to 12 tonnes.
The genus name Dystrophaeus means "coarse joint" in Greek, referencing the pitted joint surfaces that served as an attachment for cartilage.
The specific name viaemalae means "of the bad road" in Latin, referencing the arduous routes taken to find and salvage the remains.
Edward Drinker Cope noted that the joint surfaces of the limbs were thicker than the epiphyses in mammals.
The bone ends were covered by cartilage, indicating the animal grew continuously throughout its life.
Edward Drinker Cope described the fossils in the Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society in 1877 after receiving them from Joseph Leidy.
The genus Dystrophaeus was named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1877.
The type species of the genus Dystrophaeus is Dystrophaeus viaemalae.
The teeth are spatulate, a shape more typical of macronarians or non-neosauropod sauropods than of diplodocoids.
Henri-Émile Sauvage classified Dystrophaeus as a sauropod belonging to the Atlantosauridae in 1882.
Friedrich von Huene created the family Dystrophaeidae in 1904, initially assuming it contained herbivorous theropods.
Friedrich von Huene corrected his classification in 1908 to the sauropod family Cetiosauridae, refining it to the subfamily Cardiodontinae in 1927.
A recent analysis by David Gillette concluded that Dystrophaeus was a member of the Diplodocidae.
A 2015 phylogenetic analysis by Tschopp and colleagues found the phylogenetic position of Dystrophaeus to be highly unstable.
Tschopp and colleagues concluded that positions in Dicraeosauridae or Camarasauridae were equally well-supported, that it was probably not a diplodocid, and that further study was required.
Many researchers consider the taxon Dystrophaeus to be a nomen dubium.
John Foster suggests that newly found teeth and caudal vertebrae indicate that diplodocid affinities are unlikely.
The Spanish taxobox lists the family of Dystrophaeus viaemalae as Dicraeosauridae.
A modern analysis by David Gillette concluded that Dystrophaeus was a member of the family Diplodocidae.

In 2015, a phylogenetic analysis by Emanuel Tschopp, Octavio Mateus, and Roger BJ Benson resulted in classifying Dystrophaeus as a basal Dicraeosaurid, near the North American genera Suuwassea and Dyslocosaurus.
Fossils of Dystrophaeus were found in the Tidwell Member of the Morrison Formation in Utah.
Dystrophaeus lived during the Late Jurassic, specifically the Kimmeridgian stage, approximately 154 to 150 million years ago in what is now North America.
The affinities of Dystrophaeus remain uncertain due to the fragmentary nature of its only known specimen, despite excavations since 1989 uncovering more material.
